extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in foundations of mathematics; mathematicians and philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for producing and assessing pure mathematics and foundational reasoning: how to formulate definitions, axioms and proofs (use of symbolism, axiomatic method, treatment of infinity/continuity, and geometry) to achieve rigor and avoid hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/general form of propositions (pure mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure mathematics consists entirely of assertions to the effect that, if such and such a proposition is true of anything, then such and such another proposition is true of that thing. It is essential not to discuss whether the first proposition is really true, and not to mention what the anything is, of which it is supposed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mathematical work as deductions from hypotheses that are intentionally abstract and not about particular objects; separate pure-mathematical deduction from applied-mathematical questions of truth or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit rules of inference / formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: We start, in pure mathematics, from certain rules of inference, by which we can infer that if one proposition is true, then so is some other proposition. These rules of inference constitute the major part of the principles of formal logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make inference rules explicit and use them as the foundation for deductions; ensure that proofs follow from stated inference rules rather than implicit reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic formalism to reveal hidden premises
rubrics_metrics.description: People have discovered how to make reasoning symbolic, as it is in Algebra, so that deductions are effected by mathematical rules. Symbolism is useful because it makes things difficult... Then we set up certain rules for operating on the symbols, and the whole thing becomes mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt symbolic notation to prevent the temptation to rely on intuition or self-evidence; use formal manipulation to expose what must be taken as premises and what can be proved. Anti-pattern: relying on natural-language obviousness instead of formal derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize primitive notions and reduce to logical primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to learn the whole of Arithmetic, Algebra, the Calculus... we must start with a dictionary of three words. One symbol stands for zero, another for number, and a third for next after... All future symbols are symbolically explained by means of these three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reduce theory to a small set of indefinable primitives (preferably logical primitives) and explicit axioms; show how complex notions are defined from them. Strive for minimal, well-chosen primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scepticism toward self-evidence; prove the obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often by no means self-evident that one obvious proposition follows from another obvious proposition; so that we are really discovering new truths when we prove what is evident by a method which is not evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept intuitive or self-evident statements without proof where appropriate; proving apparently obvious claims can reveal falsehoods and refine understanding. Anti-pattern: treating obviousness as a substitute for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ill-defined infinitesimals; base calculus on limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Weierstrass, by strictly banishing from mathematics the use of infinitesimals, has at last shown that we live in an unchanging world... The Calculus required continuity, and continuity was supposed to require the infinitely little; but nobody could discover what the infinitely little might be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using informal infinitesimals; instead formulate calculus via rigorous epsilon–delta/limit notions (or equivalent rigorous foundations). Example: Weierstrass' approach replaces infinitesimals with limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of infinity (Cantor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of terms is infinite when it contains as parts other collections which have just as many terms as it has. If you can take away some of the terms of a collection, without diminishing the number of terms, then there are an infinite number of terms in the collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact definitions (e.g., using one-to-one correspondences / bijections) for infinite sets; do not rely on hand-wavy or contradictory intuitions about infinity. Use Cantor's cardinality ideas to settle paradoxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish cardinal and ordinal notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting gives us what mathematicians call the ordinal number of our terms... The fundamental infinite numbers are not ordinal, but are what is called cardinal. They are not obtained by putting our terms in order and counting them, but by a different method which tells us whether two collections have the same number of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with infinite collections, choose and state explicitly whether you are using ordinal or cardinal concepts; apply the appropriate methods (order-based vs bijection-based) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bijections (one-to-one correspondences) to compare sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is some relation which, like marriage, connects the things in one collection each with one of the things in another collection, and vice versa, then the two collections have the same number of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish equal cardinality via explicit bijections; use constructive correspondences as the method for comparing infinite set sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and reject misapplied finitary maxims in infinite contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim in question is, that if one collection is part of another, the one which is a part has fewer terms than the one of which it is a part. This maxim is true of finite numbers... But when we come to infinite numbers, this is no longer true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question intuitions valid for finite cases when extending them to infinite cases; identify which principles fail for infinities and adjust axioms/definitions rather than forcing contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define continuity via order rather than quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of continuity depends upon that of order, since continuity is merely a particular type of order... The notion of a limit, which is fundamental in the greater part of higher mathematics, used to be defined by means of quantity... But nowadays the limit is defined quite differently... Only order is now relevant to limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate continuity and limits in terms of order-theoretic properties where appropriate (as Cantor and modern treatments do) rather than relying on vague quantitative approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat geometry as an axiomatic family of systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry is a whole collection of deductive sciences based on a corresponding collection of sets of axioms. One set of axioms is Euclid's; other equally good sets of axioms lead to other results. Whether Euclid's axioms are true, is a question as to which the pure mathematician is indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing or evaluating geometry, state the chosen axiom system and deduce consequences within it; be explicit that different axiom sets yield different geometries and that truth in empirical space is a separate matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on figures/diagrams in formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the best books there are no figures at all. If a figure is used, all sorts of things seem obviously to follow, which no formal reasoning can prove from the explicit axioms, and which, as a matter of fact, are only accepted because they are obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let intuitive diagrams substitute for explicit axioms and formal derivations; use figures only as heuristics and ensure every claimed consequence is derivable from stated axioms. Anti-pattern: trusting diagrammatic 'obviousness' that conceals unstated assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce concepts locally and explicitly rather than assuming wholes
rubrics_metrics.description: One great advance... has been made by introducing points as they are required, and not starting, as was formerly done, by assuming the whole of space... we begin with the following axioms: (1) There is a class of entities called points. (2) There is at least one point. (3) If a be a point, there is at least one other point besides a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build theories by introducing the minimal objects and axioms needed, step by step, instead of presupposing an entire ambient space; prefer local, constructive axiomatizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make axioms explicit—avoid hidden axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Countless errors are involved in [Euclid's] first eight propositions... A vastly greater number of axioms, which Euclid unconsciously employs, are required for the proof of his propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit proofs to identify any unstated assumptions; ensure that all steps in a deduction are supported by explicit axioms or proved lemmas. Example anti-pattern: Euclid's unspoken intersection axiom in Proposition I.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize formalism and correctness over intuitive intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The most remarkable result of modern methods in mathematics is the importance of symbolic logic and of rigid formalism... Such rude shocks to mathematical faith have produced that love of formalism which appears, to those who are ignorant of its motive, to be mere outrageous pedantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor methods that guarantee correctness even if they sacrifice immediate intuitive clarity; accept formalism as a tool to avoid slipshod reasoning. Balance pedagogy with rigor but not at the cost of hidden errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern set-theoretic and relation-algebraic tools (Logic of Relatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new branch of logic, called the Logic of Relatives, has been invented to deal with topics that wholly surpassed the powers of the old logic... The investigation of different kinds of series and their relations is now a very large part of mathematics, and it has been found that this investigation can be conducted without any reference to quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ relation algebra, set-theoretic and order-theoretic machinery to handle structures previously intractable to syllogistic logic; use these tools to formalize series, order-types, and continuity.
